comments.author: Tade0
comments.story: UK professor says smearing yogurt on your windows can cool your home
comments.why: Guide to cooling paint from common ingredients with explanation
comments.text: There's an interesting guide on how to make radiative cooling paint from common ingredients complete with an explanation why it works: [VIDEO] The catch is that such paint is not particularly robust, much less weatherproof. Beats yogurt I guess, which tends to smell as it turns in sunlight. I have roof windows and was wondering how much I could gain from panels painted like that, but most likely as much as I would using the next best thing - a window sunshade, which I'm using already.

comments.author: pfdietz
comments.story: Is air conditioning making cities hotter?
comments.why: DIY example of sub-ambient cooling surfaces
comments.text: I want to point out that to optimize for temperature reduction, you want to minimize absorption while maximizing thermal radiation. This says you want the surface to be reflective at wavelengths below some cutoff, but perfectly emissive (that is, black) above that wavelength. (Actually it's a bit more complex, because the atmosphere emits IR in some bands.) Some work on surfaces of this kind have shown promising results, being able to fall below ambient temperature even in full sunlight. Do it yourself: [VIDEO]
